ideas.topic: ABS: Why You Can Steer While Slamming Brakes
ideas.angle: ABS releases and re-applies brake pressure about 15 times a second, so the wheels never lock and the car keeps steering around the obstacle. Without ABS, the car slides straight into the barrier.
ideas.hook_line_en: Your car's brakes switch on and off 15 times every second.
ideas.why: It fits the engine's scenes exactly (brake_skid vs brake_swerve, then xray_orbit, xray_brakes and xray_cabin) and it has a surprising number up front.

ideas.topic: Why Slamming the Brake Pedal Makes It Vibrate
ideas.angle: The pedal shudder that scares many drivers is the ABS pump working. It means the system is saving you, so don't lift your foot.
ideas.hook_line_en: When your brake pedal shakes in an emergency, most drivers do the one thing that can kill them.
ideas.why: xray_cabin shows the pedal vibration directly, and the point about not lifting your foot is practical and easy to share.

ideas.angle: A tyre only has a limited amount of grip. A sliding tyre uses all of it for braking, so none is left for steering. That is why the car goes straight even when the wheels are turned.
ideas.hook_line_en: Turn the steering wheel all the way, and a locked-wheel car still goes straight.
ideas.why: brake_skid shows the front wheels turned while the car slides straight, which is a surprising visual that backs up the physics.

ideas.topic: Wheel Speed Sensors: The Car's Hidden Reflexes
ideas.angle: Each wheel has a sensor that reports its speed to the ECU hundreds of times a second. The ECU spots a locking wheel before the driver can feel it.
ideas.hook_line_en: Your car notices a skid before you do, in a fraction of a second.
ideas.why: xray_orbit was built to show sensors and wires glowing to the ECU, so the explanation matches the visuals.

ideas.topic: How ABS Became Mandatory: A Short History
ideas.angle: ABS began in aircraft and was later fitted to cars. Laws then made it standard, and fact cards show the years and the number of lives saved. India's two-wheeler ABS rules can be the payoff.
ideas.hook_line_en: A safety feature that began on aeroplanes is now the law on Indian roads.
ideas.why: Year and number cards in fact_card carry the history, and the final real-life payoff and comment question suit the CTA. The exact years and figures need checking before the script is written.

The 'WHY?' beat comes right after a question. If the question beat runs long, viewers may leave before the skid footage.
The fact_card is late (about 45s). The swerve payoff before it has to hold attention until then.

facts.claim: ABS stops wheels locking by cutting brake pressure when a wheel is about to lock, so the driver can keep steering. A sensor reads each wheel's speed.

In a hard stop a valve reduces pressure and a pump restores it, in a repeating cycle. One source (HowStuffWorks) gives the rate as up to about 15 times a second, depending on the system. The script says 'daadaapu 15' (about 15) and the title says 'up to'.
The driver feels the pulsing as pedal vibration. They should press firmly, keep steering, and not pump the pedal.

The 1978 Mercedes-Benz S-Class (W116), developed with Bosch, was the first production car offered with electronic ABS. Some sources note earlier systems such as Chrysler's Sure Brake in 1971, so the script says 'modatisaari' (first time) only for this Mercedes electronic system, not 'first ever'.
